children: By Ben Cohen | Photography by Samuel Schalch for WSJ
Caspar Coppetti has a curious way of moving through life.
"I see the world feet up," he says.
It's a useful point of view for the executive who founded On, which looks from any angle like it's taking over the world.

When he runs, he's scouting other people's sneakers. When he walks through airports, he's studying the shoes other travelers have chosen for maximum comfort. On the night he met his wife, the first thing he noticed about the woman he would marry was her footwear.
"I was lucky," Coppetti tells me. "She was wearing a pair of Ons."
These days, it seems like everyone is wearing a pair of Ons.

The company that began in Switzerland with a pair of scissors and some garden hose is now conquering America. If you don't already own a pair or three, you have definitely seen them. The shoes are known for their clean design, lightweight feel and unmistakable soles, including some with those hollow pods that resemble a toothy smile. They help soften each landing, which means the very thing that makes Ons recognizable is also what makes them so comfortable.

That combination is enormously valuable. Since it went public five years ago, the company has exploded to more than $3.5 billion in annual sales. Along the way, On became a household name among runners and a fixture at the office and school drop-off.
At this stage, companies like On often feel pressure to keep growing, even if it means doing the opposite of everything they did to get there. On's executives refuse to do anything of the sort.
They're lacing up their Clouds to tread one of the finest lines in business: becoming more popular without becoming any less premium.

They're also trying to pull this off while the footwear industry is feeling pain. In August, On reported its slowest quarterly revenue growth as a public company and watched its stock drop 20% in a single day. So when the company recently welcomed investors to its Zurich headquarters, Coppetti knew what they were thinking.
"Some of you may have walked into this room with a question on your mind," he said. "Is On just a growth story, or is there more to it?"

On's executives spent the past few weeks presenting their answer to that question. First they signed Kylian Mbappé to lead a push into the soccer business. Then they unveiled something even more important for the company's future than one man's graceful feet.
They call it the On Premium Playbook.

The company's blueprint for success is full of all the usual stuff about obsession and radical innovation and validation from the best athletes in the universe. But the most revealing part of the On Premium Playbook is about basic economics-and how the company can get bigger without getting cheaper.
The classic Ons cost $160, and the average price of its footwear has shot up to $170, which is among the industry's highest. On's executives plan to keep it that way.
"We're educating our consumer not to expect a sale," Coppetti told investors.

This education began a few years ago when Nike and Adidas stepped back from traditional retail to sell directly to consumers, clearing shelf space for upstart brands like On and Hoka. By the time the sneaker giants came to their senses, they had already ceded that prime real estate to the unfamiliar, funny-looking products that have invaded our closets.

By now, Ons are no longer just for hardcore runners. They have become office attire and might as well be part of the dress code at country clubs. If you walk around the Masters, you'll pass more Ons than azaleas. The company is even chasing the affluent shoppers who have been priced out of the luxury market. If they can't afford an Hermès bag or another pair of Chanel flats, they might just splurge on a different kind of status symbol.
In the sneaker business, it can be tempting for fast-moving brands to flood the market with shoes. It's also the fastest way to cheapen a brand.

But sticking to a strategy of restraint gets harder in times of weaker demand. On's stock took a pounding after the recent earnings call when the company said it deliberately sent fewer shoes to retailers to maintain its pricing power-and keep those shoes from ending up on sale.
Even before they had any shoes to sell, On's founders believed less could be much, much more.

Like so many startup origin stories, this one begins in a garage. According to company lore, a retired Swiss triathlete and Ironman champion named Olivier Bernhard couldn't find a running shoe that met his needs, so he made one himself with a garden hose, scissors and glue.

As he tinkered, he told David Allemann and Caspar Coppetti about his experiments, and they were hiking in the Swiss Alps when they decided to take on a more grueling uphill challenge: starting a company.

Their first office back in 2010 was Allemann's kitchen, where they pored over shoe prototypes and financial spreadsheets. As they researched the market, they realized there was an opening at the very top end. Serious runners were spending very serious money on running. If it helped them get faster or feel healthier, they cared more about the quality of a product than whatever it might cost.
"They were basically willing to pay for progress," said Coppetti, now the co-CEO with Allemann.
For their very first mood board, they collected images of sleekly engineered products that command a premium: the iPhone, the Eames chair, the Dyson vacuum cleaner.
"The vacuum cleaner that performs like a jet engine," Allemann said, "and sells at five times the category price."
While it may feel like these sneakers inspired by vacuum cleaners are now everywhere, the truth is they are nowhere close. The entire planet knows Nike. To most people, On is still a preposition.

The brand's awareness went from 12% to 30% over the past three years, according to company data, and the target for the next three years is 50%. To the company's executives, the fact that so many consumers are unaware of On just means there are lots of shoppers waiting to slip into their first pair.
And the guy who sees the world feet up is always looking for his next customer.

When I sat down with Coppetti, I left my Ons at home and went with a pair of Stan Smiths made by Adidas. He spotted them instantly. In fact, he later told me that he'd clocked my shoes from across the hotel lobby before we were even introduced. He also pointed out that a person near me was in a sneaker called the Roger, named for another tennis player. As the picture of Swiss elegance and killer performance, Roger Federer was the natural face of On.
We went on discussing how Ons have become the unofficial sneakers of airport lounges when, suddenly, Coppetti looked down.
"By the way," he said. "If you change from your Stans into the Roger, you would feel much better."
